newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel, banks in basic accord.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel, banks in basic accord.

text.p: The English Channel tunnel's operator, Eurotunnel Plc, said Wednesday it agreed in principle to restructure debts equivalent to $13.6 billion on which it has not paid interest since 1995.
Eurotunnel said the plan will go to its board and banks by the end of the week and it expected details to be released next week, when trading in its suspended stock will be allowed to resume.
The debt accord must still be approved by two-thirds of its bank lenders and a qualified majority of two-thirds of its 750,000 shareholders in the landmark tunnel link between France and Britain.

A French group representing Eurotunnel SA shareholders, the Association de Defence des Actionnaires d'Eurotunnel (Adacte) said in a statement that an agreement at the last minute after 12 months of talks meant the company had incurred 5 billion francs ($968 million) in interest and blamed the banks for holding out so long.
Adacte said it appointed a specialist in corporate recoveries, Eric Habib, to analyse the agreement.
Any debt restructuring requires a qualified majority of shareholders.

Another coalition, the Eurotunnel Shareholders Association, said it was asking for a meeting with Eurotunnel so it could decide its position. The association said it has put together 32 percent of voting rights, nearly enough to block the agreement.

Eurotunnel, which has been fighting a savage fare war with rival ferry companies since it opened in 1994, froze payments to 225 banks on its 70 billion franc ($13.6 billion) debt in September 1995, unable to cope with the loans and cost overruns incurred during construction.

"The co-chairmen of Eurotunnel, Sir Alastair Morton and Patrick Ponsolle, and the steering group of Eurotunnel's syndicate of banks consider that agreement has been reached on the basic principles of the restructuring plan which is essential for the group's (company's) financial recovery," Eurotunnel said.
The refinancing involves initially converting part of the debt into equity and an issue of convertible bonds, sources close to the deal said.
One source said "definitive elements" of an accord were in place but would be made public after the Eurotunnel board and a 24-member group of "instructing banks" approve the plan.
He said Eurotunnel shares, suspended Monday in Paris, London and Brussels, Belgium, should resume trading by Tuesday once the deal has been approved and the details published.

The president of the Paris commercial court said he took the initiative to persuade a reluctant Eurotunnel and its bankers to accept the court-driven mediation which led to the breakthrough in debt negotiations.
Court President Jean-Pierre Mattei said he was motivated by considerations of fairness to shareholders and the sheer scale of the financial and legal complications if Eurotunnel failed.

"The scale of Eurotunnel is such that a failure, with its 70 billion francs (debt), an international treaty, two courts involved -- London and Paris -- would have meant a legal and financial imbroglio without precedent," he said in an interview.
"I do not believe one can or should abandon on the roadside 750,000 shareholders who placed their confidence in the banks and in a European project as extraordinary as Eurotunnel."
Morton and Ponsolle agreed on the pact with six banks which represent the 225 banks in Eurotunnel's syndicate.
But eventually each bank must ratify the complex terms, and that could take months. For technical reasons, shareholders will not be able to vote on the deal until early next year.

Although Eurotunnel reached an outline deal last May, talks became deadlocked on the pricing of the debt conversion as the company sought to protect shareholders from a massive stock dilution which would come from an unacceptably low price.
A Paris Eurotunnel shareholders' group said it wanted to meet the company's management in the next few days so that it could decide its position on the deal.
